question.prompt: Four distinct circles are drawn in a plane. What is the maximum number of points where at least two of the circles intersect?

solutions.explanation:
Two distinct circles intersect in at most two points, so begin by counting pairs of circles. Label the circles \(1,2,3,4\). Circle \(1\) has three possible partners with larger labels, circle \(2\) has two, and circle \(3\) has one. This counts each unordered pair exactly once, giving
\[
3+2+1=6
\]
pairs. Every intersection point belongs to at least one pair, so there can be at most
\[
2\cdot6=12
\]
distinct intersection points. A point shared by three circles would be counted repeatedly in the pair count, so attaining this bound requires avoiding such coincidences.

To attain the bound, place four centers on a straight line, one unit apart, and draw a circle of radius \(2\) about each center. Every pair of centers is \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\) units apart. These distances are positive and less than the sum of the radii, \(4\), so every pair of circles intersects twice.

No three of these circles share a point. To see why, take any three centers in their order along the line and call them \(X,Y,Z\). A point on all three circles would be equally distant from \(X,Y,Z\), so it would lie on the perpendicular bisectors of both \(XY\) and \(YZ\). Those bisectors are distinct parallel lines and cannot meet.

Consequently, all two-per-pair intersections are distinct. The maximum is \(\boxed{12}\), choice D.
